A candle on a table should meet your eye, not sit above it.

The flame belongs below the eyeline of the people seated, or above their heads. Anywhere in between it blinds, and two guests facing each other stop looking at each other. Below means a candlestick of twenty centimetres, not forty.

They are lit when the first guest walks into the room. Never before.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in Tuscan villas, cloisters and historic houses that have no kitchen of their own.

Twelve at a table that does not stand still.

Everything on a boat is laid for movement: nothing round, nothing tall, glasses with a low centre, cloth weighted at the corners rather than clipped. The galley is four square metres, so the cooking happens ashore and only the finishing happens here.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number one.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We bring the brigade and the field kitchen into places that have neither.

The bloom on a grape is not dust, and it does not wash off.

That pale film on the skin is wild yeast. It sits there on its own and it is what ferments the fruit. A bunch that arrives shining is a bunch that has already been washed, which means it is already a few days old.

So it comes into the kitchen like this, and it goes onto the table like this.

We bring the brigade and the kitchen. The room goes back the way we found it.

A cigar outlasts any dessert.

Forty minutes, and forty minutes in which nobody stands up: whoever opens one has decided to stay. It needs air that moves and an amaro that can carry smoke, and it is not the moment for coffee.

The kitchen has already been taken apart. Nobody in the other room notices.

A cloister is a room with no roof and four walls of shade, which is why it works in September and stops working in the middle of October.

Fifty covers fit down the centre. The paving takes a trolley, the arcade takes the service line, and the sky decides everything else.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number two.

A ripe fig tells you by weeping.

When it is ready it loses a bead of syrup at the eye and the skin splits on its own. Pick it the day before and neither happens; the day after, you find it on the ground. The window is about forty-eight hours.

Which is why in September figs are bought in the morning and served the same evening.

The same cloister, eight hours later.

Thirty covers down the middle, and every plate came through the arcade carried, because nothing rolls on paving laid in the fifteenth century. The kitchen is two rooms away and nobody at this table will ever see it.

It is not a venue. It opens for one evening, and then it closes again.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number two, at night.

Nobody pours for a toast standing up.

The glasses are filled before anyone is asked to raise one, because twenty people lifting glasses while somebody is still moving behind them is how a jacket gets ruined. Two of us go round the outside, never between the chairs, and it takes under a minute.

Then everybody is holding something at the same time, which is all a toast really is.

It is laid to be walked on wet and scrubbed with salt water, and it marks under anything with a point. Trolleys do not come aboard: every plate arrives carried, up a passerelle with a handrail on one side only.

A porcino is judged by the stem, not by the cap.

If the stem gives under your thumb the mushroom is gone, and the grub only shows when you open it. Which is why they are bought whole and opened one by one, and why at least one in ten is thrown away. The price already accounts for that.

The good ones never arrive all at once.

A courtyard behind a town palazzo is the only quiet square metre in the middle of a city.

The gate is the whole problem. Everything that goes in goes through it, and the paving is old enough that the wheels have to be large ones: small castors drop into the joints and stop dead.

A table lit only by candles is lit from below.

It flatters everything on it and nothing above it, so whatever matters sits low and the centre stays under fifteen centimetres. Tall arrangements are how a room ends up dark with a bright stripe down the middle of it.

The one thing you never do is add a lamp to fix it.

The same courtyard, after sunset.

Twenty-four covers, and all the light is on the table: the walls climb eight metres and nothing reaches above four. It is the easiest room in the dossier to light, and the one where you watch the forecast until the last afternoon.

A private courtyard in the centre of a city is not for hire. You ask for it.

What goes wrong at an important dinner is almost never the cooking. It is being the fourth event of that Saturday.

A terrace has one advantage and one problem, and they are the same thing.

Nothing above it. Which means the light is right until it is not, and the whole evening is built around a single hour: drinks outside, dinner inside, and a changeover rehearsed because it has to happen in the time it takes to serve one round.

White truffle is bought by weight, and it is lost by weight.

From the moment it comes out of the ground it loses weight every day, and what leaves is water: the truffle weighed on Monday is not there on Saturday. It is kept at four degrees wrapped in paper, and the paper is changed daily.

It is never cooked. It goes on at the last second, and the plate underneath has to be hot.
